messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai arrived for her first session with the clinical description of a ship captain, a job she had worked toward since she was eighteen, but the woman who sat in the chair looked more like someone bracing for a storm than someone who commanded a vessel. She was twenty-three, single, Southeast Asian American, and she spoke in short, clipped sentences, her eyes scanning the room the way she scanned the radar at night. The traumatic event was not a single moment but a childhood that stretched like a long, dark hallway. Her father, her primary caregiver, had been physically abusive throughout her early years. She remembered the belt, the back of his hand, the way he would wait until her mother was out of the house. She remembered the dark. He always came at night, when the house was quiet, when she was already in bed. She learned to sleep with one eye open, to listen for the creak of the floorboards, to map every shadow in her room. The darkness itself became a signal: something bad was about to happen.

As she grew older and left home, she thought she had left that fear behind. She threw herself into maritime training, into the discipline of navigation, into the bright, fluorescent-lit world of a ship’s bridge. But the fear had not left. It had only learned to attach to new things. Now, as a captain, she found herself unable to sleep without a light on. Nighttime, or waking up in the dark, sent a spike of cold terror through her chest. Her body went tense, her muscles coiled, ready to react to danger that was not there. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, that danger could come from anywhere, that she was somehow defective, broken in a way that other people were not. She felt isolated from her crew, set apart by something she could not name. When she drove with other people in the car, she felt trapped, her eyes darting to the rearview mirror, her hands gripping the wheel, her mind racing through escape routes before the car even left the dock. She always identified escape routes before she felt comfortable anywhere—every restaurant, every meeting room, every hallway on her own ship. Being alone with a male crew member, even for a routine briefing, made her stomach clench. She would keep the door open, position herself near the exit, and feel the threat rise in her throat like bile. These triggers did not just happen to her; they confirmed what she already believed. The darkness, the car, the man—each one was proof that the world was unsafe, that she was right to be afraid. And because she believed the world was dangerous, she saw danger everywhere. Every shadow became a threat. Every closed door became a trap. The cycle tightened.

Over the months, she began to avoid situations that might trigger her. She stopped accepting rides from colleagues, even when it was practical. She insisted on driving herself, even when exhausted. She rearranged her watch schedule to avoid being alone on the bridge with certain male officers, inventing reasons that sounded professional but felt hollow. She stopped going to social gatherings after dark. The isolation she already felt deepened. Her crew noticed. They called her cold, distant, unfriendly. She did not correct them. What she felt was not coldness; it was a constant, humming readiness for violence. Her body was on alert all the time. She had strong negative feelings—fear, shame, anger—that rose without warning, sometimes in the middle of a calm conversation. She could not explain them. She thought there was something fundamentally wrong with her, that she was defective, that other people did not live like this. The threat she felt made the world seem more dangerous, and the dangerous world made her feel more threatened. She was trapped inside a logic that never let go.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment on the bridge, three weeks ago. It was night. The sea was calm. She was alone with a male deckhand who was simply reviewing the log. He did nothing wrong. But her body went into full alarm. She felt her heart pound, her breath shorten, her vision narrow. She had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood shaking over the sink, staring at her own face in the mirror. She realized she could not keep living this way. She was afraid of the dark, afraid of her own crew, afraid of the job she had worked her whole life to earn. She came to therapy because she wanted to stop running. But what frightened her most was the possibility that she was right—that the world really was that dangerous, that she really was that broken, and that no amount of talking would ever make the darkness feel safe again.
